sections.start: People who had never met were paired for half an hour of video conversation.
sections.how: Describes the setup and states the headline findings about rising mood and underestimated liking.

sections.start: The mood ratings trace a very simple shape: a flat, slightly nervous opening, then a steady climb that is still going when the call ends.
sections.serves: Across 1,656 conversations the mood climbs from the first minute to the last — and people consistently walk away believing they were liked less than they actually were.
sections.how: Reports positive affect and arousal both rising at the four time points.

sections.start: The rise is not driven by a few ecstatic outliers.
sections.serves: The mood ratings trace a very simple shape: a flat, slightly nervous opening, then a steady climb that is still going when the call ends.
sections.how: Shows most conversations finish higher and gives typical and median gains, so the climb is broad.

sections.start: Split the conversations by how the pair felt before the call and the pattern is sharp.
sections.serves: The mood ratings trace a very simple shape: a flat, slightly nervous opening, then a steady climb that is still going when the call ends.
sections.how: Shows lower-starting pairs gain more and both ends converge near 7.

sections.start: After the call each person answered two symmetric questions: how much do you like this person, and how much do you think this person likes you?
sections.serves: Across 1,656 conversations the mood climbs from the first minute to the last — and people consistently walk away believing they were liked less than they actually were.
sections.how: Compares own liking 5.99, expected liking 5.35, and actual partner liking 5.99.

sections.start: So the room is full of mutual warmth that neither side registers.
sections.serves: The expectation was wrong: the partner's own answer, averaged over the same pairs, was also 5.99 .
sections.how: Quantifies the person-by-person perceived-liking gap averaging 0.64 points.

sections.start: 54.9% of people underestimate how much their partner likes them.
sections.serves: So the room is full of mutual warmth that neither side registers.
sections.how: Reports that a majority underestimate, while fewer overestimate or are accurate.

sections.start: The asymmetry is systematic rather than random noise: if people were merely guessing badly, underestimates and overestimates would be equally common.
sections.serves: 54.9% of people underestimate how much their partner likes them.
sections.how: Argues the direction of error is skewed toward underestimation, so it is not random.

sections.start: The same caution shows up in how people think they were seen.
sections.serves: The asymmetry is systematic rather than random noise: if people were merely guessing badly, underestimates and overestimates would be equally common.
sections.how: Shows the same underestimation pattern in intelligence and kindness ratings.

sections.start: The pairs differed in sex, race, age, education and politics, and the study recorded each difference.
sections.how: Reports that demographic differences correlate only weakly with enjoyment.

sections.start: What does predict it is whether the two people felt they were experiencing the same thing.
sections.how: Reports shared reality correlates far more strongly with enjoyment and liking than demographics, and enjoyment ranking tracks affect gains.

sections.start: Partners rated each other on a set of traits on the same 1-to-9 scale, and the profile is lopsided.
sections.serves: They rate their partner more intelligent ( 7.68 ) and kinder ( 7.98 ) than they believe the partner rates them ( 7.06 and 7.43 ): they hand out generous judgements and assume a stingier verdict comes back.
sections.how: Lists high warmth traits and low humour, supporting generous warmth ratings.

sections.start: That the lows are rated far below the average is its own signal: the worst moment of a conversation averages 5.80 , the best 7.83 , and the overall impression 7.32 .
sections.how: Reports worst, best and overall moment ratings.

sections.start: Each conversation produces two independent accounts, and they do not match.
sections.how: Reports average partner differences in affect, arousal and shared reality.

sections.start: Who does the perceiving matters as well.
sections.serves: Each conversation produces two independent accounts, and they do not match.
sections.how: Shows loneliness correlates with expected liking but not liking given, so perceiver traits affect reports.
